Oath

OHTH (rhymes with both) · noun

Hear It

What It Means

a formal promise spoken out loud in front of other people, often at a big ceremony

The new mayor raised her right hand and took an oath to serve the city.

Worked Example

In court, the witness took an oath to tell the truth before answering any questions.

The witness spoke the promise out loud, in a serious place, in front of everyone. A spoken, formal promise like that is an oath.

Antonyms

joke

lie

lie: words that are not true

How Strong Is It? — Promise → oath → Contract

Promise vs. oath

Promise vs. oath: Promise is lighter: you can make a promise to a friend anywhere, even on the bus.

Contract vs. oath

Contract vs. oath: Contract is stronger: a contract is written and signed, and breaking it can bring real trouble with the law.

Put it together

Put it together: Oath is one of the oldest words in English. It came straight from Old English, and it has no prefix, root, or suffix to peel apart.

Use the root in a new word: swear

Use the root in a new word: swear: In court, people swear an oath to tell the whole truth.

Word Choice

Oath goes with big, formal moments: judges, mayors, and team captains take an oath out loud while others watch. You say it - you don't usually sign it.
